In discussions about choosing distros, I see the usual mentions of Ubuntu, Mint, Arch, and even sometimes the odd Fedora, but I never hear anything about Antergos.

Isn't it just Arch with a simplified installer and an extra repo?
Why is Antergos almost never mentioned?
I usually see Manjaro plugged as the "easy to install Arch". I just haven't heard much about Antergos at all.
It has a great installer, Manjaro is also never mentioned.

I was just thinking that - Manjaro got me on Arch (migrated from the deb world). KDE Manjaro is seriously impressive, after a long time on XFCE and not really feelin' Gnome it floored me how well developed and cohesive modern (5.x) KDE is.
Usually I don't mention Antergos because installing it means restarting 20 times hoping that Cnchi installer can make it past partitioning the hard drive before crashing.

Second this, they don't have enough redundancy in cnchi. Almost every time I install I run into a different problem; most recently I had an issue that required me to edit the antergos mirrorlist to only download from the official repo. A newbie is not going to know how to troubleshoot these kinds of errors. That being said, I love antergos it's arch for lazy people.
Using cnchi was a horrible experience. I had at least five major problems with it that prevented me from installing everything successfully.

I think the primary reason is the number of different distributions available. There are A LOT of them. Typically you only hear about the distros with the highest number of users. Personally I like Fedora on my server (its basically the Red Hat playground), Ubuntu on my notebook, and Raspian on my Raspberry Pi 2.
By their nature, rolling distros aren't user friendly. New users want stability.

I feel Manjaro is more beginner friendly than Antergos, and a user ready for an Arch install is either able to install it manually or would rather use installation scripts or something like evo/lution.

Because it's treated like the red-headed stepchild of distributions.

Arch users, in and of themselves, pride themselves in knowing what they're doing. The install process being part of this knowledge.

The very nature of Arch requires this knowledge since it's the "bleeding edge" of software, and updates aren't necessarily the most stable. In other words: updates can break your machine, and you're going to have to know how to fix them.

Antergos and Manjaro both offer the pacman package manager that Arch uses (so, potential problems) but install the system for you (so you don't necessarily need to know how your system works).

This can cause multiple problems when an update breaks your system and you don't know what happened or how to fix it... Or any problem arises, for that matter:

First, the Antergos/Manjaro communities are relatively small. And, the majority of those small communities is composed of people who chose these distro BECAUSE they didn't understand Arch. So, if you go to them with an Arch-related question (e.g. - an update breaking something), the likelihood that they won't understand, or your question will go unanswered is pretty high. This lack of community support is bad, and is why Ubuntu still has so many users, and attracts new users everyday, even though they're the LEAST secure and sell your desktop space as ads.

Second, if you try to reach out to the Arch community as an Antergos/Manjaro user, and they find out you "cheated" your way through the install, they will most likely stop helping you. Again, they pride themselves of being well-acquainted with their machines, and running an installer isn't that...

So, given the potential lack of support from both communities, and the risk of problems later down the line, I never suggest one of those two distros. If the user is capable, I suggest Arch. If they're not, I suggest a Debian based (apt get, usually more stable) distro for them. But I NEVER suggest Manjaro or Antergos to anyone.

The only place I use one of those two is on a VM, where I don't want to go through the whole install process just to delete the machine in an hour... So I run something in an installer, do what I need to do, then delete the VM.

If they're not, I suggest a Debian based (apt get, usually more stable) distro for them. But I NEVER suggest Manjaro or Antergos to anyone.

I think this is sad. I really like the Arch distro, but prefer Manjaro because I don't need to go through every step of installation, and then setting up and configuring everything. If the distro wants to grow, it should be more welcoming and not so high-and-mighty.

I don't understand what you see as "high-and-mighty" from the fact that a distro which requires you to have Linux experience facilitates users which require the same thing.

I also think you're misinterpreting what I said... I don't actively discourage Manjaro/Antergos... But I NEVER actively encourage it's use, unless it's for someone like me, using it JUST for a virtual machine. In that case, the initial setup isn't important and any bugs can just be deleted, and the system started over... But, for a daily driver, I refuse to recommend Antergos or Manjaro to an inexperienced user since, as I said above, the likelihood of the not receiving quality help is pretty high.

I also think you're looking at Manjaro and Antergos as being equivalent distros to Arch, but with a graphical installer... And this could not be more untrue. Both use proprietary package repositories, which differ from the Arch repos (one is more guilty of this than the other). These are NOT true Arch distros, and encouraging their use is NOT encouraging Arch growth. Saying it is encouraging Arch growth is like saying that encouraging Mint use helps the Ubuntu ecosystem grow, since they're both Debian based. Both distros are built and installed differently, and the pull from different repos, which is why they're different distros... Which is the exact same situation as Arch and Manjaro/Antergos.

Because it's not very popular. For the same reason you don't hear about Antergos, you won't hear about Manjaro or openSUSE.

The general public has a tendency of following the line of what they've been told by the media, in this case tech "journalism" sites which are for the most part filled with lazy, incompetent, uneducated shitheads being paid by Microsoft to place Windows 10 native advertisements as genuine articles. Sure, there are very competent UNIX veterans writing for some of the sites, but these are mostly smaller sites aimed at professionals and general public doesn't go there.

They push the Ubuntu and Mint because they're on top of distrowatch page and they're too lazy to scroll down. Hence, Ubuntu, Mint, sometimes Debian and Fedora articles being dragged for years to the point those are the only distros ever being mentioned on popular sites. Oh, and you want to be a top dog hacker? Go install Arch! Let's face it, Arch is a distro difficult to install, configure and maintain if you don't have at least 5 years experience as a Linux administrator. A lot of people just copy and paste stuff from the Arch wiki, but in order to truly understand what is going on behind those commands you need years of experience. Again, lazy journos think copying and pasting counts the same as understanding.

That's why.

Because Arch is already niche enough - all its derivatives (Antergos, Manjaro, etc.) are even more niche, so the only way you find out they exist is by reading the documentation (which Arch users should be used to anyway :P).

It's the same with Sabayon - it's virtually unheard of, even though most people have heard of Gentoo.
